lectures.name: Intro to Diabetes
lectures.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
lectures.framing: Both types are diagnosed by the same glucose thresholds — what separates them is the mechanism producing the hyperglycemia: absolute autoimmune insulin deficiency vs. a spectrum of insulin resistance and relative deficiency.
lectures.keypoints: the alpha cells are spared in T1DM — the lesion is beta-cell specific. Autoantibody count, not presence, is what carries risk (1 = background risk, 3 = 40% in five years). GAD is the specific marker. Monozygotic concordance is higher in T2DM (90%) than T1DM (50%) — the counterintuitive fact worth remembering. And the octet explains why T2DM needs combination therapy: each drug class corrects a different defect.

lectures.name: Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.title: Approach to New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.framing: The whole diagnosis turns on one question: are symptoms present? If yes, a single abnormal glucose is sufficient — do not delay treatment for a confirmatory test.
lectures.keypoints: symptoms present → one abnormal glucose diagnoses diabetes; no symptoms → two are needed. The DCCT trial logic underlies everything here — intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia, a trade-off now partly offset by pumps and CGM. Glucose gel works through buccal mucosa, so it can be given when swallowing is unsafe.

blocks.html: Workup skeleton

• Hx — the three classic early symptoms nearly every patient has: polyuria (including nocturia / new bed-wetting), excessive thirst, weight loss despite unchanged or ↑ appetite. Then screen for late/severe features: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, hyperventilation, fatigue, ↓ level of consciousness.
  • PEx — hydration status, weight loss, level of consciousness, Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath.
  • Ix — random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1, urine dipstick for glucose and ketones, serum C-peptide (is she making any insulin?), ABG if DKA suspected. ⚠ FPG and A1c are usually unnecessary here — the diagnosis is already clear.
  • Tx — insulin + structured education; treat DKA emergently if present.
  • Follow-up — annual urinalysis for albuminuria (diabetic nephropathy screening).

lectures.name: Pharmacology of Insulin
lectures.title: Insulin Preparations
lectures.framing: Choose a preparation based on what the insulin is covering — a meal (bolus) or the fasting state (basal). Onset and duration are set by one thing: how fast monomers dissociate from the hexamer, since insulin binds its receptor only as a monomer. Anything that stabilizes the hexamer (zinc, protamine, self-aggregation, albumin binding) → slower onset, longer duration.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Analogues are NOT more effective at lowering HbA1c than human insulin — they are safer and more convenient (faster onset, better postprandial match, lower variability, less nocturnal hypoglycemia). Only regular insulin can be given IV. Basal insulins must never be used in pumps, and most basal insulins must not be mixed with another insulin before injection. Insulin does not interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other drugs — but drugs that alter glucose metabolism (e.g. steroids ↑ hepatic glucose production) change how well it works. Exogenous insulin is imperfect because physiological secretion is glucose-dependent, and that fine-tuning is lost.

lectures.keypoints: the suppression/stimulation pairing is the single most testable idea here — excess is tested by trying to turn it off, deficiency by trying to turn it on. primary adrenal insufficiency loses both cortisol AND aldosterone, which is what separates it from central causes. lectures.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology
lectures.title: Diagnosing T2DM and the Grey Zone
lectures.framing: T1DM and T2DM share identical diagnostic thresholds — so the diagnostic work is (1) crossing the threshold, (2) deciding how many measurements you need, and (3) working out which type you are looking at.
lectures.keypoints: symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. Do not diagnose during acute illness (MI, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery. C-peptide and anti-GAD move in opposite directions between the two types: low C-peptide + high anti-GAD = T1DM. >90% of all diabetes is Type 2; 589M adults live with diabetes worldwide (~1 in 9), ~43% of them undiagnosed, and ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes. Finally — a T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent: weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range, though it can recur, so keep checking a few times a year.

lectures.keypoints: abdominal pain and vomiting = DKA, not HHS. Hours = DKA, days = HHS. T1DM = DKA, older T2DM = HHS. lectures.name: Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes
lectures.title: Glycemic Goals of Care
lectures.framing: The target is never a single number — it is a negotiation between preventing long-term complications and avoiding hypoglycemia now. Tight control buys microvascular benefit; severe hypoglycemia carries ↑ mortality.
lectures.keypoints: severity of hypoglycemia is defined by whether the patient can treat it themselves — not by the glucose number. A1c is the best-validated marker of control but lags, so it never replaces glucose readings when you are actively changing therapy. CGM measures interstitial, not blood, glucose. Tight control helps microvascular outcomes most; the macrovascular gain is smaller and slower — and in T2DM, blood pressure control is what drives CV risk down.

lectures.name: Introduction to Obesity
lectures.title: Obesity — Assessment and Management
lectures.framing: Obesity is a complex, progressive, relapsing chronic disease — abnormal or excessive body fat that impairs health. BMI alone does not predict adiposity-related complications; stage the impact, not just the number.
lectures.keypoints: tirzepatide (dual GLP-1/GIP) beats semaglutide beats naltrexone-bupropion for weight loss. The most serious post-bariatric deficiency is thiamine — give it before any glucose or you precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. The BMI cut-off drops to 25 for South and East Asian patients. EOSS stages the functional impact, which is what determines bariatric referral — not BMI alone. Ghrelin is the only fasting/hunger hormone here; everything else in the list promotes satiety. The pharmacotherapy stopping rule is 5% at 12 weeks. Gastric banding is explicitly not recommended. Retinopathy that worsens in pregnancy usually settles after delivery without permanent damage, but screen pre-conception, during, and within the first postpartum year. Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern.

lectures.name: Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology
lectures.title: Thyroid Hormone Synthesis & Calcium Homeostasis
lectures.framing: Two axes, one shape: a gland reacting to a single sensed variable. For the thyroid the sensed variable is circulating T3/T4, read by the hypothalamus and pituitary, and the step the exam turns on is that iodination comes FIRST, then coupling. For the parathyroid the sensed variable is ionized Ca2+, read directly by the chief cell's CaSR, and the step it turns on is that ⭐ there is no PTH receptor in the gut — PTH raises absorbed calcium only indirectly, through calcitriol.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Iodination precedes coupling, and iodide entry is active transport (NIS, then pendrin), never passive diffusion. ⭐ The goitre of iodine deficiency is not the gland "trying harder" — it is loss of negative feedback → sustained TSH-receptor drive → follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia, and maternal deficiency is the #1 cause of preventable intellectual disability worldwide. ⭐ somatostatin inhibits TSH ONLY, not PTH. Calcium is the single discriminator between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and hypocalciuria is what separates FHH from primary. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is anti-TPO, blocking iodination of thyroglobulin, treated with levothyroxine; Graves disease is an activating anti-TSH-receptor antibody with exophthalmos. 99% of body calcium sits in bone as calcium phosphate, and of the 1% in blood 50% is free/ionized — that is the only fraction the CaSR reads and the only fraction that acts.

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
lectures.title: Approach to Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
lectures.framing: The whole evaluation runs on one test in one direction: ⭐ serum TSH to case-find, free hormone only to confirm and grade. TSH works because primary disease, at the gland, is by far the most common kind, and there TSH moves opposite to the hormone. ⚠ That logic inverts in central disease, where pituitary TSH is the broken part and moves with the hormone. Then one further question splits thyrotoxicosis into its causes: is the gland making hormone, or leaking it? — which is what radioactive iodine uptake answers.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ TSH case-finds, free hormone confirms — and the only reason to break that order is suspected central disease, where TSH and FT4 go together and TSH moves WITH the hormone. ⭐ RAI uptake answers why, not whether. High uptake = the gland is synthesizing; low uptake = hormone is leaking out of it or coming from a bottle, and low-uptake disease is treated supportively while you watch for the hypothyroid phase. ⭐ Goiter symmetry is a free discriminator: symmetric points to Graves, asymmetric to nodular disease, and thyroiditis can have no goiter at all. ⭐ Methimazole is first line for Graves and RAI is first line for nodular disease, because only Graves remits. Levothyroxine's 1-week half-life is why TSH is rechecked at 4 to 6 weeks and not sooner. anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, and ultrasound are the tests to leave alone in straightforward hypothyroidism.

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism
lectures.title: Hyperparathyroidism, Hypoparathyroidism & the Calcium Panel
lectures.framing: You do not diagnose these from the calcium. You diagnose them from the pattern across four analytes at once: PTH, calcium, phosphate, vitamin D. ⭐ Always send a PTH with any abnormal calcium, because PTH is the branch point: high or inappropriately normal means the parathyroid is driving it; suppressed means something else is. ⭐ In hypocalcemia, phosphate is the branch point instead. And before any of it, correct for albumin — an uncorrected number sends you down the wrong branch.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Correct for albumin, then always send PTH — those two steps decide the whole workup, and the deck's own worked example (Ca 2.6 with albumin 20) corrects to 3.0, straight past the admission threshold. ⭐ Fractional excretion of calcium separates FHH from primary hyperPTH: under 0.01 is FHH, over 0.02 is primary — but 20% of FHH lands in the 0.01–0.02 overlap, and the result is only interpretable off thiazides for 3 months, with a normal magnesium and a 25-OH-D above 50. ⭐ In hypocalcemia, phosphate is the discriminator: high phosphate is a PTH problem, low phosphate is vitamin D — and vitamin D deficiency is the commoner of the two. Age cuts both ways in hyperPTH: under 50 is a reason to operate, over 50 and asymptomatic is a reason not to. ⭐ Loop diuretics treat hypercalcemia and thiazides cause it, but thiazides are the right drug in chronic hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia will not correct while magnesium is low, and magnesium at either extreme can cause hypoparathyroidism.

blocks.html: $$\huge corrected\ calcium = measured\ calcium + 0.02(40 - measured\ albumin) $$

Normal serum calcium 2.15–2.55 mmol/L, of which ⭐ the ionized fraction is 1.1–1.3 mmol/L (50%) and is the only part that acts; protein-bound is 0.9–1.1 (40%) and complexed 0.18 (10%). Every 1 g/L of albumin away from 40 shifts calcium by 0.02. hypercalcemia is corrected Ca > 2.55; hypocalcemia is < 2.1. ⚠ Symptoms track both the absolute value and its RATE OF RISE, which is why a slowly climbing calcium is often silent.

blocks.html:
Treatment of hypercalcemia — admit if corrected Ca > 3 mmol/L.

1. Volume repletion — assume a 4–6 L deficit, replace with normal saline.

2. Forced diuresis — 4–10 L of NS plus furosemide plus K+, ⚠ only once well hydrated. ⭐ LOOP diuretics only, NEVER thiazides — thiazides cause hypercalcemia.

3. bisphosphonates — IV zoledronate.

4. calcitonin — ⚠ tachyphylaxis at 24–48 h, so it is a bridge, not a treatment.

5. prednisone 40–60 mg/day then taper — because steroids ↓ activation of vitamin D: for myeloma, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity. Dialysis is the last resort.

Treatment of primary hyperPTH: asymptomatic and over 50 → no treatment. Drugs for bone protection: bisphosphonates, denosumab, estrogen / HRT, cinacalcet. ⭐ Keep them well hydrated and avoid thiazides and lithium. Symptomatic → surgery.

parathyroidectomy is indicated when any one of these holds: Ca > 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit · bone mineral density T-score < −2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip, or ⅓ radius · vertebral fracture · creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min · 24-hour urine calcium > 10 mmol/day with ↑ stone risk · nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis · ⭐ age < 50.

Treatment of hypocalcemia — reserved for corrected Ca < 1.9 mmol/L plus neurological (tetany, seizure, carpopedal spasm) or cardiac (prolonged QT) symptoms.

- Acute: 1–2 g of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 mL of 5% dextrose over 15–20 min → 1–3 mg/kg/h elemental calcium → cardiac monitoring and admission → ⭐ treat coexisting hypomagnesemia, because the calcium will not correct until the magnesium does.

- Chronic (same as treating hypoparathyroidism): calcitriol 0.25 mcg b.i.d., monitoring calcium and phosphate, keeping 25-OH-D > 75 nmol/L · 1–2 g elemental calcium in divided doses · ⭐ thiazides here, to ↓ calcium excretion and lower stone risk · recombinant human PTH (rhPTH), approved in the US and Europe.

- ⚠ Aim for the LOW-normal range and monitor for ectopic calcification: renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis, head MRI for basal ganglia calcification, and keep the calcium-phosphate product under 4.4 mmol²/L².

lectures.name: Pathology of Thyroid Masses
lectures.title: Thyroid Masses: Clinical Evaluation and Pathology
lectures.framing: Most thyroid nodules are benign (0.1% annual incidence, 10% lifetime probability), so the job is not to find cancer in every nodule but to stratify which nodule earns a biopsy and which biopsy earns an operation. ⭐ Four inputs stack into one decision: clinical risk, biochemistry, imaging, and FNAB — together they give risk-adapted management, and none of them is read alone. The order is fixed: TSH first, because a low TSH sends you to a radioactive iodine scan before any ultrasound — ⭐ a HOT nodule is never cancer and stops there, while a COLD nodule comes back to the ultrasound and is scored like any other nodule.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ TSH is the first test, because a low TSH diverts you to an RAI scan and a hot nodule is benign; a normal or high TSH goes to ultrasound and TI-RADS. ⭐ FNA cannot tell a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma (identical nuclei, and only invasion separates them), but ⭐ it diagnoses papillary carcinoma outright, because in PTC the nuclei are the diagnosis. ⭐ Graves makes papillary projections without atypia — architecture alone does not mean papillary carcinoma. ⭐ Amyloid in a thyroid tumour is calcitonin, and means medullary carcinoma, which is RET point mutation while PTC is RET-PTC translocation. ⭐ Anaplastic carcinoma is what a well-differentiated cancer becomes, and it is the one that will not take up iodine. Needle core biopsy is the wrong instrument for the neck, and punch biopsy is for skin. Child, male, first-degree family history, and neck radiation are the clinical risk factors that raise the pre-test probability before any imaging.

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis
lectures.title: Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Risk and Treatment
lectures.framing: ⭐ You can diagnose osteoporosis three ways, and only one of them involves a bone density scan. A fragility fracture alone is enough, whatever the BMD says. That is the whole point of the treatment gap: a fracture is the diagnosis, and ⭐ only 15% of patients are treated after a fragility fracture, against 80% who get a beta blocker after a heart attack. Once diagnosed, treatment choice turns on which fracture site you need to prevent and whether the patient has already failed or been harmed by an antiresorptive.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis on its own — but skull, hands, feet and ankles do not count, and neither does a genuinely traumatic fracture. ⭐ T-score compares to a young adult, Z-score to age-matched peers; only the T-score diagnoses. ⭐ raloxifene and teriparatide have no hip fracture data — reach for a bisphosphonate, denosumab, or estrogen when the hip is the concern. ⭐ Every anabolic course must be followed by an antiresorptive, at 1 year for romosozumab and 2 for teriparatide. ONJ has a definition with a clock in it: exposed bone unhealed at 8 weeks, and dental work goes first. Groin or thigh pain in a patient on a bisphosphonate is an impending atypical femoral fracture, not arthritis.

lectures.name: Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease
lectures.title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Osteomalacia, Paget's & Osteogenesis Imperfecta
lectures.framing: Three diseases of bone that are not osteoporosis, and ⭐ the lab panel separates all three before any imaging. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect from vitamin D deficiency, so calcium and phosphate fall and ALP rises. Paget's is disordered remodelling, so calcium and phosphate stay normal while ALP goes very high. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen gene defect, so the panel is normal and the diagnosis is clinical. ⚠ Osteomalacia is routinely mistaken for osteoporosis, and the tell is that osteomalacia has overt symptoms while osteoporosis is indolent.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ ALP is the thread through all three: very high in Paget's, high in osteomalacia, normal in OI. ⭐ Calcium and phosphate are BOTH low in osteomalacia and BOTH normal in Paget's — that pair alone separates them. ⭐ Urine calcium is LOW in osteomalacia, which is the opposite of what a stone-former's panel looks like. ⭐ Proximal myopathy is the osteomalacia feature that osteoporosis never has, and it is what causes the falls. ⭐ Bone-forming drugs are contraindicated in Paget's — you do not encourage a formation process that is already disordered, which makes zoledronate the answer and teriparatide the trap. ⭐ Increased hat size and warmth over a bone are Paget's, and blue sclerae with fractures from birth are OI. A young adult with celiac disease, falls, weakness and pseudofractures has osteomalacia, not osteoporosis.

Complications of Paget's disease: fractures · hypercalcemia with immobility · cranial nerve compression → deafness · spinal cord compression · ⭐ osteosarcoma in 1–3%, signalled by marked bone pain, a new lytic lesion, and a rising ALP · ⭐ high-output congestive heart failure from increased vascularity · osteoarthritis.

When to treat Paget's, even in an asymptomatic patient, given active disease (↑ ALP or scintigraphy showing active lesions): disease in the skull, long bones, spine, or bone abutting a joint · ⭐ a surgical procedure planned in a pagetic site, because the lesions are vascular and can hemorrhage · ⭐ coexisting congestive heart failure, which Paget's vascularity can worsen.

Lifelong monitoring in osteogenesis imperfecta: growth and head circumference and yearly spirometry (restrictive lung disease from the skeletal deformity) · hearing test, BMD, ECG and echocardiogram every 2 years · skeletal radiographs every 1–2 years · neurologic and cranial assessment as symptoms indicate. Treat the bone disease when there are long bone deformities, vertebral compression fractures, or more than 3 fractures per year.

lectures.framing: Two halves that share one idea: ⭐ structure tells you what can go wrong there. In the histology half, the epithelium at each site predicts its disease — keratinized skin gets skin cancers, and the one place two epithelia meet is the one place cervical cancer starts. In the embryology half, ⭐ the same teratogen does something completely different depending on the week it arrives, so timing, not the agent, is what the question is really testing.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Keratin and adnexa separate labia majora from minora, and that is the whole histological question. ⭐ The transformation zone is where two epithelia meet, which is why it is where cervical cancer arises and why the cancer can be of either type. ⭐ Tubular glands mean proliferative and oestrogen; tortuous secretory glands mean luteal and progesterone. ⭐ The functionalis sheds and the basalis rebuilds it. ⭐ Fertilization happens in the ampulla, and the ampulla is also where an ectopic most often implants — same widest segment, same reason. ⭐ The zona pellucida must degenerate before implantation can happen. ⭐ Syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG; hCG maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over at week 8. ⭐ Every germ layer descends from the epiblast, and the hypoblast only ever makes the yolk sac lining. ⭐ Weeks 3 to 8 is the critical period — before it, all or nothing; after it, minor anomalies only.

lectures.name: Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
lectures.title: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
lectures.framing: The axis is three tissues and one non-negotiable requirement: ⭐ GnRH must arrive in PULSES. A continuous GnRH signal does not amplify the axis, it shuts it down, which is exactly how a GnRH agonist becomes a chemical castration. Everything else follows from two anatomical facts: ⭐ the median eminence has no blood-brain barrier, so hypothalamic peptides can leave the brain, and ⭐ parvicellular neurons feed the ANTERIOR pituitary through a portal system while magnocellular neurons bypass it into the POSTERIOR pituitary.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pulsatility is the whole axis. Continuous GnRH suppresses, which is why an agonist ends up doing the same job as an antagonist but with a dangerous surge first. ⭐ **kisspeptin is the strongest positive input to the pulse generator, and ⭐ steroids never touch the GnRH neuron directly — they work through interneurons. ⭐ LH → theca and Leydig; FSH → granulosa and Sertoli, and inhibin brakes FSH alone. ⭐ The shared α subunit is why the β subunit is what gets measured. ⭐ Cholesterol to pregnenolone, in the mitochondrion, is the rate-limiting step. ⭐ Estradiol and progesterone act without further metabolism; testosterone usually does not. ⭐ Estradiol induces the progesterone receptor**, so the order of the cycle is built into the receptors themselves.

lectures.name: Approach to the Menstrual Cycle
lectures.title: The Menstrual Cycle
lectures.framing: One hormone does something no other hormone in the body does: ⭐ estradiol switches its own feedback from negative to positive. Below threshold it suppresses FSH; held above 300–500 pg/mL for about 48 hours it flips to feed-forward and triggers the LH surge. That single switch divides the cycle in two, and everything else is bookkeeping around it: the follicular phase is built by FSH and dismantled by the estradiol it produces; the luteal phase runs on progesterone and lasts a fixed two weeks unless an embryo arrives.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Estradiol is the only hormone here that reverses the sign of its own feedback, and it needs both a level (300–500 pg/mL) and a duration (~48 h) to do it. Getting one of those two right and the other wrong is the classic distractor. ⭐ FSH falls during the follicular phase — counter-intuitively, because the follicle it grew is now making the oestrogen that suppresses it. ⭐ The luteal phase is the fixed half of the cycle; when a cycle is short or long, it is the follicular phase that varies. ⭐ The corpus luteum regresses after two weeks unless an embryo rescues it, and that regression is menstruation. ⭐ Aromatization happens in the granulosa cell, on an androgen the theca cell made — remember which receptor sits on which cell and the rest follows.

The evidence that each piece is necessary, from the deck's two experiments:

- ⭐ GnRH pulses are sufficient to start a cycle. A 24-year-old with Kallmann syndrome — who makes no GnRH — had a spontaneous ovulatory menstrual cycle initiated by an invariant intermittent subcutaneous GnRH infusion, 25 ng/kg every 2 hours for 27 days. Invariant is the point: the pituitary and ovary generate the cycle's shape, given only a steady pulse train.

- ⭐ The ovary carries the cycle, not the brain's anatomy. Ovarian tissue transplanted subcutaneously to the abdomen of a castrated male rhesus monkey showed repetitive ovulatory cycles averaging 28 days.

lectures.title: Testicular and Ovarian Function
lectures.framing: ⭐ The two gonads are the same machine with different settings. In both, LH acts on the steroid-making cell (Leydig, theca) and FSH acts on the nurse cell (Sertoli, granulosa), and in both the nurse cell makes inhibin to brake FSH. What differs is the output: ⭐ spermatogenesis makes 4 haploid gametes continuously from a self-renewing stem cell; oogenesis makes 1 from a reservoir that was finished before birth. That single asymmetry explains menopause, polar bodies, and why the two arrest points exist at all.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Map the four cells onto two hormones and you have the lecture: LH → Leydig and theca (androgen); FSH → Sertoli and granulosa (inhibin, and aromatase in the ovary). ⭐ 4 gametes from spermatogenesis, 1 from oogenesis, and the female reservoir is fixed before birth. ⭐ The oocyte is arrested twice: prophase I until recruitment, meiosis II until fertilization — fertilization is a trigger, not just a fusion. ⭐ The blood-testis barrier exists because sperm are genetically foreign to their own host. ⭐ Most FSH receptors wins the dominant-follicle competition, and ART simply removes the competition by flooding the system. ⭐ The granulosa cell trades FSH receptors for LH receptors as ovulation approaches — the same cell, answering to a different hormone. ⭐ 5-α reductase makes DHT for hair, glands and external genitalia; aromatase makes estradiol and closes the growth plates. ⭐ Only 5% of testosterone is free, and only that 5% works.
